scenario.name: Bounded mTLS C2 foothold, host survey, command execution, and small transfer
scenario.scope: Generate and run one Windows beacon, establish contained mTLS C2 only to Kali, perform bounded discovery and one benign shell task, and download one fixed non-host-data marker.

linux_extension.transport_comparison: The HTTPS beacon and raw mTLS session had identical JA3, JA3S, and all-zero JARM in this v1.7.3 run. HTTPS was distinguishable by repeated short connections at the configured cadence; mTLS session mode held one 60.057947-second flow. Clear HTTP exposed its request profile, DNS exposed encoded A/TXT query bursts, and neither had TLS fingerprints.

upstream.conclusion: Nothing upstream characterises a Sliver Linux implant behaviourally. The upstream Sliver-labelled Linux rules identify operator binary names or selected callback ports, while the implant was renamed and used operator-selected ports. Windows rules cannot cover the Linux implant.

detection_limitations: Generated names, hashes, ports, transport profiles, and TLS stacks are operator- or version-dependent; no rule hardcodes the lab address or port.

JA3/JA3S can overlap with other Go software and can change across Sliver/Go versions; HTTPS and mTLS were identical here, so use flow shape, periodicity, and endpoint context rather than claiming transport discrimination.
Single-event Sigma cannot express the observed 10+0–3 second flow or DNS-burst periodicity; an analytics layer must aggregate by endpoint pair/profile or by DNS source and terminal parent domain.
The clear HTTP User-Agent and URI profile are operator-configurable; HTTPS encrypted those request fields and therefore could not be evaluated against the HTTP-profile rules.
TLS 1.3 HTTPS and mTLS exposed no passive certificate chain/x509 row in these Linux traces, and both active JARM measurements were all-zero.
Linux endpoint and Zeek/Suricata rules are not testable on the Windows EVTX corpora; precision is classified qualitatively from run-local positive evidence and production false-positive reasoning.
The broad no-SNI/no-visible-cert Zeek rule is intentionally a low-level hunt and requires aggregation/tuning.
The DNS rules identify an observed restricted-alphabet multi-label encoding rather than Sliver exclusively; legitimate DNS tunnels can match, and a custom encoder can evade them.
